name: Rapid shallow breathing index
seoDesc: Rapid shallow breathing index: work out RSBI from the respiratory rate and the tidal volume. A free health calculator with the formula, units and a worked…
summary: Give the Rapid shallow breathing index calculator the respiratory rate and the tidal volume and it returns RSBI. Think of it as a shortcut for an informed starting point to take to a clinician, not a diagnosis. Press Calculate for the answer; change a value and it steps off screen until you press again, so each edit can be judged on its own.

sections.title: How does the Rapid shallow breathing index calculator work?
sections.html:
The Rapid shallow breathing index calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports RSBI in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the respiratory rate and the tidal volume.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A number, expressed in breaths/minute.
  • A number, expressed in ml.

sections.title: What are the variables at a glance?
sections.html:
Everything the page asks for and everything it reports, side by side. The roles matter: a value you supply is read from the form, a calculated value is derived from the others and cannot be set directly.

FieldWhat it isUnitRole
Respiratory rateA number stated in breaths/minute.—You supply it
Tidal volumeA number stated in ml.—You supply it
RSBIA plain number, with no unit.—Calculated

sections.title: The formula behind the Rapid shallow breathing index calculator
sections.html:
One relationship drives the whole page:

RSBI=(1000 × respiratory rate ÷ tidal volume)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Respiratory rate = 10 and Tidal volume = 10. Working through the relationship above gives RSBI = 1000.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: RSBI = 1000 should be roughly the size you expected from Respiratory rate = 10 and Tidal volume = 10.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• A number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Rapid shallow breathing index calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Deciding whether a reading is worth a second look
  • Preparing for an appointment so you can describe your numbers clearly
  • Tracking a measurement over time and understanding what changed
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the respiratory rate and the tidal volume — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the Rapid shallow breathing index calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

sections.title: How do you check the answer yourself?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time — respiratory rate for instance — and watch which results move. A result that stays put does not depend on it.
  • Try a round value you can work out in your head. If the answer matches your mental arithmetic, the inputs are on the scale you assumed.
  • Re-enter the same figure and confirm the result is stable; a number that moves when you press Calculate again is a sign that a field is still empty.

faq.q: What does the Rapid shallow breathing index calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns RSBI, derived from the respiratory rate and the tidal volume. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Rapid shallow breathing index calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the respiratory rate and the tidal volume, which is 2 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports RSBI = 1000. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Rapid shallow breathing index calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. The calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.
